The paper argues that in the post conflict city, the issue of identity and its relationship to place is central.

(1) the city centre of Belfast has a long history of political violence; (2) the city centre has been the focus of a number of regeneration projects since the 1980s; (3) the Peace Walls are the most visible symbols of the conflict; (4) there is a lack of public debate about how to deal with the Peace Walls; and (5) the Peace Walls have become a symbol of division and segregation, and a barrier to social integration.
the built environment of the city of Belfast is a product of the history of the city and the history of Northern Ireland.

the city of Belfast has been, is, and will be a place of contestation and struggle.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to develop a new discourse for the Belfast built environment that avoids the politics of identity and the politics of exclusion.
the city is a place where people live, work, play, shop, learn, and so on, and where the built environment is the physical manifestation of the social, economic, and political life of the city.
we have developed a model for the design and management of urban environments in which the social construction of space is central.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the built environment of a city, especially in a post conflict setting, is an important site for the expression of identity and a key factor in the construction of a city’s identity.
a city vision for Belfast needs to be inclusive, and needs to be based on the city’s past, present and future.
the city is not just a place, it is also an identity, and that identity can only be changed by a process of dialogue and engagement.
